eras.name: Rules
eras.background: Early translation and language programs were built from hand-written dictionaries and grammar rules. Demos looked promising, but the rules broke on real text, and a critical US report cut funding for machine translation.

eras.name: Counting
eras.background: As more text went online, researchers replaced rules with statistics counted from data. Search ranked documents by weighted word counts, and speech recognition and translation estimated probabilities of word sequences. The counts treated words as unrelated symbols, which capped how far they could go.

eras.name: Word vectors
eras.background: Neural networks learned a dense vector for each word, so words used alike ended up close together. Once training became cheap, pretrained word vectors replaced hand-built features as the input to NLP models.

eras.name: Seq2seq
eras.background: Instead of pipelines of separately tuned parts, one network learned to map an input sequence to an output sequence. Attention let it look back at the input, and the Transformer then dropped recurrence altogether.

eras.name: Pretraining
eras.text: Pretrain once, adapt to many tasks
eras.background: Labeled data stayed scarce, but raw text was plentiful. Models pretrained on huge corpora and then fine-tuned beat task-specific models almost everywhere, and bigger models kept doing better.

eras.name: LLMs
eras.background: Scaled-up pretrained models could handle new tasks from instructions alone. Chat assistants brought them to the public, and most NLP research moved to large language models.

nodes.label: Rule-based MT
nodes.problem: Translating Russian research by hand was slow.
nodes.idea: The Georgetown–IBM demo translates Russian sentences with a small dictionary and a few grammar rules.
nodes.impact: Hopes ran high, but rules never scaled and US funding was cut after the ALPAC report.

nodes.label: TF-IDF
nodes.problem: Keyword search treated every word as equally important.
nodes.idea: Spärck Jones weights a word by how rare it is across documents; multiplied by its frequency in a document, that is TF-IDF.
nodes.impact: The standard way to score search results for decades, later refined into BM25.

nodes.label: N-gram LM
nodes.problem: Speech recognizers needed to know which word sequences are likely.
nodes.idea: Estimate the next word's probability from counts of the previous few words.
nodes.impact: Powered speech recognition and translation for decades, but could not generalize to unseen phrases.

nodes.label: Statistical MT
nodes.idea: IBM learns translation probabilities from aligned English and French parliamentary text.
nodes.impact: Data-driven translation replaced rules and led to phrase-based systems such as early Google Translate.

from.why: Hand-written rules could not cover real language, while large bilingual texts were becoming available.

nodes.label: Neural LM
nodes.idea: A neural network learns a vector per word and predicts the next word from those vectors.
nodes.impact: Introduced learned word embeddings, though it was too slow to train on large corpora.

from.why: Counts treat every word as unrelated, so a phrase never seen in training gets no probability.

nodes.label: word2vec
nodes.idea: Shallow skip-gram and CBOW objectives learn word vectors quickly from billions of words.
nodes.impact: Pretrained word vectors became the default input to NLP models.

from.why: Sparse word counts cannot tell that two different words mean similar things.
Its word vectors were useful, but training it on web-scale text was far too slow.

nodes.label: Seq2seq
nodes.idea: One LSTM encodes the source sentence into a vector and another decodes the translation.
nodes.impact: Showed a single network could translate end to end.

from.why: Phrase-based systems stitched together many separately tuned parts.

nodes.label: Attention
nodes.idea: Let the decoder look back at every source word and weight them at each step.
nodes.impact: Fixed long sentences and became the core operation of later models.

from.why: Squeezing a whole sentence into one vector lost detail, so long sentences translated badly.

nodes.label: Transformer
nodes.idea: Use self-attention alone, so every position is processed in parallel.
nodes.impact: Became the architecture of nearly every later language, vision and speech model.

from.why: Attention worked, but it still sat on top of recurrent networks that read one token at a time.

nodes.label: GPT
nodes.idea: Pretrain a Transformer decoder to predict the next word, then fine-tune it for each task.
nodes.impact: Started the GPT line that scaled into today's LLMs.

from.why: Predicting the next word needs no labels, so any text can train a model.
Supplied an architecture that trains efficiently on huge corpora.

nodes.label: BERT
nodes.idea: Pretrain a bidirectional Transformer encoder by predicting masked words.
nodes.impact: Contextual embeddings became the default for classification and search.

from.why: Each word had one vector, so a word like bank meant the same thing in every sentence.
Supplied an encoder that attends to the words on both sides at once.

nodes.label: Dense retrieval
nodes.idea: Encode questions and passages with BERT and retrieve by vector similarity.
nodes.impact: Embedding search became the retrieval half of RAG and LLM applications.

from.why: Its embeddings capture the meaning of whole passages, which keyword matching misses.

nodes.label: ChatGPT
nodes.idea: Tune a GPT model on instructions and human preferences and serve it as a chat app.
nodes.impact: Brought language models to a mass audience, and NLP research moved to LLMs.

from.why: Larger GPTs knew a great deal but continued text instead of following requests.

main.title: Stanford CS224N: Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning
main.why: Word vectors, parsing, language models, translation, Transformers and pretraining. In English.

main.title: Simple, Proven Approaches to Text Retrieval
main.why: Raw term counts favor long documents, so BM25 combines IDF with saturating term frequency and length normalization, still Elasticsearch's default.

further.title: Term Weighting Approaches in Automatic Text Retrieval
further.why: Not every word matters equally for retrieval, so TF-IDF weights each term by its frequency in the document and its rarity in the collection.

main.title: Two Decades of Statistical Language Modeling: Where Do We Go from Here?
main.why: N-gram language models were the workhorse of speech recognition and translation, and this survey covers perplexity, smoothing and the fixes tried for their weaknesses.

main.title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model
main.why: N-gram models cannot generalize to unseen word sequences, so this neural language model learns word vectors that share statistics across similar words.
Neural language models were too slow to train on large corpora, so word2vec learns word vectors with the simple skip-gram and CBOW objectives.

further.title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation

main.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
main.why: Neural networks needed fixed-size inputs and outputs, so seq2seq uses one LSTM to encode the source sentence and another to decode the translation.

main.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
main.why: Squeezing a sentence into one fixed vector hurt long translations, so attention lets the decoder search the source at every step.

main.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
main.why: A fixed word vocabulary cannot cover rare words, so BPE splits them into frequent subword units.

main.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training
main.why: Labeled data is scarce, so GPT pretrains a Transformer decoder on unlabeled text and fine-tunes it for each task.
Left-to-right pretraining sees only the left context, so BERT pretrains an encoder that reads both directions by predicting masked words.

further.title: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach
DistilBERT, a Distilled Version of BERT: Smaller, Faster, Cheaper and Lighter
Unsupervised Cross-lingual Representation Learning at Scale
DeBERTa: Decoding-enhanced BERT with Disentangled Attention
Smarter, Better, Faster, Longer: A Modern Bidirectional Encoder for Fast, Memory Efficient, and Long Context Finetuning and Inference

main.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
main.why: GPT-2 shows that a large language model trained on web text handles many tasks zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning.

further.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
further.why: Transfer learning methods were hard to compare, so T5 casts every task as text in, text out and tests pretraining choices one at a time.

main.title: Connectionist Temporal Classification: Labelling Unsegmented Sequence Data with Recurrent Neural Networks
main.why: Speech data rarely has frame-level alignments, so CTC trains a recognizer directly on audio and its transcript.

main.title: wav2vec 2.0: A Framework for Self-Supervised Learning of Speech Representations
main.why: Transcribed speech is scarce, so wav2vec 2.0 pretrains on unlabeled audio and fine-tunes on a small labeled set.
Speech models trained on clean benchmarks broke on real audio, so Whisper trains on a vast amount of weakly labeled web audio and works without fine-tuning.

main.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
main.why: Term matching misses paraphrases, so DPR trains a dual encoder on question-passage pairs and retrieves by embedding similarity.

further.title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
further.why: Comparing sentence pairs with BERT is too slow for search, so Sentence-BERT embeds each sentence once and compares embeddings by cosine.
Term matching failed on natural-language podcast queries, so Spotify retrieves episodes with a fine-tuned multilingual sentence encoder.

main.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
main.why: Knowledge stored in model weights is hard to update, so RAG retrieves passages with DPR and has BART write answers from them.
